justice: Pedestrian space is not clearly allocated: the street edge is occupied by parked scooters and scattered items (e.g., appliances/objects along the right side), reducing equitable access for people walking.
No visible curb ramps, tactile paving, or marked accessible crossings in view, suggesting limited barrier-free accessibility for users who need step-free routes.
The roadway appears to function as shared space without clear rules/markings; this can disadvantage slower or less assertive users (e.g., pedestrians) when scooters and cars mix in the same corridor.
safety: Mixed traffic conditions: scooters/motorbikes are traveling in the same narrow carriageway as a car, with no lane markings or separation, increasing conflict risk for all road users.
Side areas are cluttered (parked scooters on the left; bulky items and uneven materials on the right), which can force pedestrians into the roadway and create trip/collision hazards.
Limited formal traffic control is visible (no crosswalks, stop lines, or traffic-calming devices apparent), reducing predictability and increasing crash risk on a residential/commercial lane.
livability: Active ground-floor frontage and small shops/signage along the left side suggest local services and some street activity that can support daily needs.
However, the presence of debris/stacked materials and outdoor storage (right side) indicates weak street management, lowering perceived neighborhood quality.
A large street tree/green mass on the right provides a natural element that can improve local enjoyment and micro-environment, though it is not integrated into a clear public space.
sustainability: High presence of scooters/motorbikes implies relatively low-space, potentially lower-emission mobility compared with car-dominant streets, supporting more efficient travel patterns.
A prominent street tree canopy on the right contributes to urban greening and potential heat mitigation, but overall tree coverage along the street edge appears limited.
No visible stormwater/green infrastructure features (e.g., permeable paving, bioswales) and the street looks fully hardscaped, limiting environmental performance.
aesthetics: Overhead utility wires are visually dominant across the streetscape, reducing visual order and perceived neatness.
Building facades appear mixed and utilitarian, with awnings and signage creating a somewhat cluttered streetscene rather than a cohesive streetscape.
Visible clutter (parked scooters, stacked appliances/objects, and uneven edge conditions) detracts from cleanliness and overall visual appeal despite some greenery.
comfort: Thermal comfort is uneven: there is substantial shade from the large tree on the right, but much of the street (left/middle) is exposed with limited continuous shading.
Physical comfort for walking is reduced by narrow/obstructed edges (parked scooters on the left; materials and objects on the right), leaving limited clear pedestrian path space.
Psychological comfort is lowered by the shared, unmarked environment where vehicles and scooters move close to pedestrians, increasing stress and reducing perceived refuge.
walkability: Sidewalks/footpaths are not clearly delineated; pedestrians may need to share the carriageway due to edge obstructions (parked scooters and street-side storage).
No visible pedestrian priority infrastructure (crosswalk markings, curb extensions, or pedestrian signage) to support safe crossings and continuous walking routes.
Irregular street edges and clutter (objects, uneven materials) create a less comfortable and less accessible walking experience, especially at the margins.
bikeability: No dedicated or protected bike lane markings are visible; cyclists would need to mix with scooters and cars in a narrow corridor.
Roadway appears constrained with multiple scooters and parked vehicles, increasing overtaking and dooring/encroachment risks for cyclists.
No visible bicycle parking or cycling wayfinding/markings; the street environment seems oriented to informal scooter parking rather than safe, legible cycling.
